subcategory.intro:
You may be the friend who can make a messy notice readable in ten minutes. That skill can earn money in the hours around another job, but a design is useful only when the right person can use it. A salon customer needs to find the service and booking number. A guest at a crowded event needs to know where to stand. A beautiful file with tiny text or the wrong date will fail both of them.

Choose one kind of small client and one deliverable you can finish after work. Ask where it will appear: a phone screen, a shop window, a printed card or a sign seen from across a room. Get the final words, dimensions, logo and approval contact before you begin. Show a rough layout, then a proof with the actual information. Check spelling, prices and dates with the client, and ask them to sign off the print version. If you use photographs or fonts, confirm you have rights for the intended commercial use.

A side service needs a boundary around revisions. Agree on the number of concepts, sizes, correction rounds, editable files and the date by which the client must respond. A last-minute text change can mean more work than the original layout. Price the thinking, test prints, travel and printer coordination if you offer it. Ask for part payment before an event job that cannot be resold if cancelled. Keep a copy of the approved proof so neither side has to rely on memory.

The ten paths below solve different small problems. Some designs must be understood at a glance; others must survive a wet market table or a small package. Choose the work where you can ask the buyer one more practical question, and where your own evenings can meet the real deadline.
subcategory.how_to_choose: Start with a business whose everyday questions you understand. If you like organising dense information, a menu or timetable may suit you. If you enjoy physical context, visit a venue and design signs at the size people will really see. Ask who supplies final copy and who pays the printer. A digital image, a print-ready file and an editable master are different deliverables. Test the result on a phone or at actual print size. Charge for one clear scope with defined revisions, and refuse a deadline that gives the client no time to check names, dates and prices before printing.

faq.q: Do I need professional software?
faq.a: You need tools that produce the formats and print quality promised. A simple design tool can handle a first project if you can check dimensions, readability and export. Be honest about the files you can deliver.

faq.q: Who checks the final spelling and prices?
faq.a: You should proofread, and the client must approve the final facts before publication or printing. Send a clear proof and record sign-off. A misplaced digit can cost more than another revision round.

faq.q: Should I provide an editable file?
faq.a: Agree on that before quoting. A print-ready file and an editable master take different preparation and may use different fonts or assets. Explain what the client will receive and can change later.

faq.q: Can I put client work in my portfolio?
faq.a: Ask permission before you post it, especially when a design includes private names, children or an unreleased offer. Agree whether you may show a public image or only describe the work.

ideas.title: Salon Service Menu Board Design
ideas.hook: You walk into a salon and still have to ask what a basic haircut includes because the wall menu is crowded.
ideas.summary: You design a readable service menu board for a neighbourhood salon owner, helping a visitor choosing a service find an answer quickly. Test a wall print and phone image at real size. A checked salon menu proof, one approving contact and a revision round keep the evening assignment ready to print or share.
ideas.what_it_is: You walk into a salon and still have to ask what a basic haircut includes because the wall menu is crowded. You ask a neighbourhood salon owner where the salon menu will appear and what a person must understand first. Then you group services, duration and approved price enquiry notes, arrange the information in a readable order and check salon menu legibility at actual display size. Get final wording, logo and dimensions for the salon menu before polishing. Show a rough salon menu layout, a proof and one point for factual approval. Do not invent a price or service promise to fill a gap. Deliver the agreed salon menu files with names the client can recognise, and keep the approved proof for later corrections.
ideas.who_pays_you: A neighbourhood salon owner pays you because prices and service names change after the board is ordered. You offer one salon a sketch made from its current menu. Show a small before-and-after example and ask what confuses a visitor choosing a service now. The salon menu buyer may have a printer or staff member, but needs someone to make scattered facts clear. Name one person who can approve the salon menu; conflicting comments can keep a modest job open for weeks.
ideas.how_money_comes: You charge per approved layout and quote reprints or updates separately. Quote the salon menu dimensions, number of layouts, revisions and file formats before beginning. Take part payment for a salon menu specific to an event or brand. Printing, installation or another salon menu size is separate unless included in the scope. A late salon menu text change after approval is new work; a mistake you introduced is yours to correct. Count the hours spent on the salon menu after your day job.
ideas.what_you_need: You need final service list, brand colours and print dimensions, rights to the fonts and images, and a tool that exports files for a wall print and phone image. Check salon menu contrast, spelling and type size where a visitor choosing a service will see it. Have a neighbourhood salon owner approve every factual detail in the salon menu. Do not invent a price or service promise to fill a gap. A salon menu test print or phone screenshot can reveal a problem your large design canvas hides.
first_30_days: Stand where a customer reads the present board.
Ask the owner which services are misunderstood most.
Make a rough grouping and test type size at real distance.
Quote a paid layout with one final proof round.
Get signed approval before sending the print file.
ideas.what_hurts: Prices and service names change after the board is ordered. Do not invent a price or service promise to fill a gap. Your salon menu may look balanced on a laptop and fail at real size. A neighbourhood salon owner may send a new service price after delivery. Keep one salon menu approval contact, a change cutoff and a dated proof. If printing changes scale or colour, help identify whether the problem was in your salon menu file or the printer's setup.
ideas.verdict: Build this if you like making a readable service menu board clear for a visitor choosing a service and can meet a real approval deadline. Walk away if the salon will not approve its real services and prices. A customer should understand the choice before sitting down.

faq.q: Should every price appear on the board?
faq.a: Follow the salon's approved menu. For variable work, explain how a customer gets a quote rather than placing a misleading fixed amount.

faq.q: What if the owner changes prices next month?
faq.a: Offer an update at a defined fee and keep the editable master organised. A reprint is separate from a text correction before approval.

faq.q: Can I use hairstyle photos from the internet?
faq.a: Use the salon's own images with permission or assets licensed for this use. A clear text menu may work better than unlicensed generic photos.
